The handoff is a complete build brief for the Anthropic Platform SWE take-home. Nothing has been built yet. The directory holds only this handoff, the seed concept, the roadmap, and an archive folder.

## What it asks for

**The idea.** Tabframe is a distributed computer whose worker nodes are browser tabs. A single hosted coordinator hands out Mandelbrot tiles over WebSockets. Each tab computes its tiles in a Web Worker and sends the pixels back. Closing a tab drops a core. The coordinator notices missed heartbeats and reassigns that tab's unfinished tiles. Finished tiles are memoized, so churn never loses progress and the image always completes correctly.

**The demo everything serves.** The build is done when a reviewer can reproduce this from one link:

1. Open the URL. One worker joins and the render starts tile by tile.
2. Spawn ten workers. Tiles fill faster and the throughput counter climbs.
3. Kill half. Nodes vanish, their tiles flash as reassigned, throughput dips then recovers, and the image finishes whole.

Both real tabs and in-app spawn and kill controls must work. The controls exist because the reviewer may only ever open one tab.

**Non-negotiables from the assignment:**

- **Deployed** to a public HTTPS and WSS URL. The reviewer installs nothing.
- **Self-contained.** No reviewer data, and the whole churn story is drivable from one page.
- **Hard cap of eight hours.** Scoping itself is graded, so cutting is a feature.
- **Visible human judgment.** The rationale has to own what was cut and why.
- **Deliverables** are a deployed prototype, a public GitHub repo with README, a roughly five-minute video plus a short written rationale, and the AI transcripts.

## Scope and invariants

**In scope:** coordinator with heartbeats and a live node set, tile dispatch with Web Worker compute, reassign-on-timeout with memoized results, a live dashboard, and spawn and kill controls.

**Out of scope:** Raft or any consensus, C to WASM upload, sandboxing, K-way voting, a RISC-V interpreter, WebRTC mesh, durable key-value storage, SharedArrayBuffer multicore, and MapReduce. These become the "how I'd extend it" story. The stated test for any feature is whether it makes the open, kill half, still correct moment more legible.

**Invariants that make it Tabframe rather than a job queue:**

- **No shared memory across tabs.** Every coordination step is a message.
- **Idempotent, at-least-once tasks.** Recompute is always safe.
- **Single-assignment, memoized results.** A done tile is never recomputed.
- **Location transparency.** Workers are addressed by node id only.
- **Thin control plane.** The coordinator holds small metadata. Pixels flow through it but are not authoritative state.
- **No error path in user code.** The runtime absorbs every worker death.

**Architecture.** One TypeScript Node or Bun process serves the static pages and the WebSocket endpoint, so there is a single deploy unit. State lives in memory as nodes, tiles, and results. The worker page connects, receives a node id, spawns a Web Worker, and heartbeats on an interval. Node loss is three missed heartbeats. The dashboard subscribes to coordinator events. Deploy target is Fly, Render, or Railway.

| Direction | Messages |
|---|---|
| Worker to coordinator | hello, heartbeat, result, ack |
| Coordinator to worker | welcome, assign, cancel |
| Coordinator to dashboard | nodeJoined, nodeLeft, tileAssigned, tileDone, tileReassigned, throughput |

## Plan and gaps

Deploy is deliberately first so the project can never end as local-only. If behind at M3, the doc says cut M4 and never M3.

| Milestone | Window | Checkpoint |
|---|---|---|
| M0 scaffold and deploy | 0:00 to 0:30 | Public WSS URL answers from a fresh browser |
| M1 spine | 0:30 to 2:00 | Dashboard shows tabs joining and leaving |
| M2 distributed compute | 2:00 to 4:00 | Image renders across multiple tabs |
| M3 failure as non-event | 4:00 to 5:30 | Kill half, image still completes, reassignment visible |
| M4 observability polish | 5:30 to 6:30 | Throughput, ledger view, colored states, flashes |
| M5 package and rationale | 6:30 to 8:00 | README, video, rationale doc, transcripts |

**Gaps I would settle before starting:**

- **In-app spawn is unspecified.** Popups get blocked, so hidden same-origin iframes are the realistic way to make in-app workers real nodes with their own sockets. Server-side fake workers would undercut the "no servers do compute" claim.
- **There is no kill message.** The protocol only has cancel. Kill half needs the coordinator to tell a tab to drop its socket and terminate its Web Worker.
- **Main-thread heartbeats get throttled in background tabs.** That produces false deaths with a three-interval timeout. Heartbeating from the Web Worker is far less throttled, and it fits the doc's wish to treat throttled as slow rather than gone.
- **Free hosting tiers sleep.** A spun-down instance can take most of a minute to wake, which wrecks the click-and-it-works moment. Pick a host or tier that stays warm.
- **The assignment PDF is referenced but not at the top level.** It may be in the archive folder. The builder should have it open alongside the roadmap.

# Tabframe — an elastic distributed computer made of browser tabs

> **Working title.** Rename freely. This document is a *seed*: hand it to a capable model in a fresh session, then drive the build with the prompt ladder at the bottom.

## North star (read this first)

Tabframe is a fault-tolerant distributed virtual machine whose compute nodes are ordinary **web browser tabs**: opening a page adds a core, closing it removes one, and the system keeps computing **correctly** through constant churn. Users **upload their own parallel programs**, which compile to WebAssembly and run against a small virtual-machine abstraction — cores, message channels, write-once memory, durable storage — that **hides where work runs and what fails**. A small set of stable nodes forms a **consensus-backed control plane** that remembers the authoritative state; the ephemeral tabs are pure workers. Each tab runs a **minimal microkernel** and coordinates only by **message-passing** — there is **no shared memory anywhere** across tabs.

The pitch in one line: *every visitor is a core; close the tab, lose the core; it keeps running — and you program it like a normal machine.*

## How to use this document

Give the "North star", "Design constraints", and "Build order" sections to the fresh session as standing context, then issue the numbered prompts one at a time, keeping each layer runnable and demoable before advancing. The constraints are load-bearing — they are what stop the design from collapsing into a slow distributed-shared-memory toy.

---

## The idea in stages

### Stage 0 — The pitch
A supercomputer with no servers doing the compute, assembled live from strangers' idle tabs, that you program as if it were one elastic machine and that survives you killing most of it mid-run.

### Stage 1 — The substrate: tabs as ephemeral cores
A tab loads a page, spins up a **Web Worker**, and registers as a node. Nodes come and go constantly and unpredictably. Reality to design around: browsers **throttle background/hidden tabs** (timers clamped, rAF paused), so node availability is not binary up/down but a **health spectrum** (fast / slow / throttled / gone). Run compute in a Worker, treat capacity as bursty, and schedule around health. A single tab is itself a multicore machine, so each node may offer several real threads (via `SharedArrayBuffer` + Workers *within that one tab*).

### Stage 2 — No shared memory: message-passing only
The only cross-node primitive is **sending a message to a logical endpoint**. Endpoints are named by **unforgeable capabilities**, never by physical location, so a send works whether the target is in the same tab (fast path) or three strangers away (network). This **location transparency** is the entire reason "code doesn't care how it happens in the background" falls out for free. `SharedArrayBuffer` is allowed *only within a single tab's own cores*, never across tabs.

### Stage 3 — Microkernel per tab, multikernel across the fleet
Each tab runs a **minimal microkernel** whose only jobs are: IPC (message-passing), scheduling local execution units, allocating local memory, and enforcing capabilities. **Everything else is a userland service** reachable only by IPC: the name/registry service, the scheduling policy, storage, and the "drivers" (WASM engine, WebSocket/WebRTC transport, IndexedDB-as-disk). The fleet as a whole is a **multikernel** (à la Barrelfish): many per-tab kernels coordinated by messages, with global state in a replicated control plane. Key insight: a microkernel's usual weakness is IPC cost, but here **the machine is already a network**, so "everything is a message" isn't a tax — it's just the medium.

### Stage 4 — The resource model (the runtime ABI users link against)
This is the make-or-break contract — design it first. User programs link a small runtime library that exposes a virtual machine:
- `spawn(task, input) -> future` — submit a unit of work; the runtime places it.
- `send(cap, msg)` / `recv(cap)` — message channels (IPC surfaced to userland).
- write-once **futures / immutable objects** — `alloc` returns a single-assignment handle; anyone with the cap reads it. **No mutable distributed state.**
- durable **KV** `put/get` — the consensus-backed store, for state that must survive total churn.
- **collectives** — `scatter / gather / reduce / barrier` for SPMD workloads.

Mental model handed to the user: *"you program a machine with N cores, fast local scratch, message channels, and a durable store — and you never learn the cores are strangers' tabs."* The same binary runs on 3 nodes or 300.

Here's what the search turned up on each part of your query:

## Binary frames & close code 1003

API Gateway WebSocket APIs don't currently support binary frames in incoming message payloads. If a client app sends a binary frame, API Gateway rejects it and disconnects the client with code 1003. The status code reference confirms this: 1003: API Gateway returns this status code when an endpoint receives a binary media type. Binary media types aren't supported for WebSocket APIs.

**Workaround:** If the client sends a text-encoded binary data (e.g., base64) as a text frame, you can set the integration's contentHandlingStrategy property to CONVERT_TO_BINARY to convert the payload from base64-encoded string to binary. To return a route response for a binary payload in non-proxy integrations, you can set the integration response's contentHandlingStrategy property to CONVERT_TO_TEXT to convert the payload from binary to base64-encoded string.

Note that the server→client direction is murkier. A re:Post thread reports that the situation for sending binary data from the server to the client is indeed less straightforward. While there isn't explicit support for sending binary frames directly over WebSockets, there are workarounds available. In that thread, the user found that with CONVERT_TO_BINARY on the integration response, if the lambda replies with base64 this leads to a client side UTF8 error. Which appears to be the API gateway sending the binary response to the client in a text type, rather than binary type websocket frame.

## Quotas: message size, frame size, connection duration, idle timeout

An AWS blog summarizes the key limits: connection duration of 2 hours, idle connection timeout of 10 minutes, message payload size of 128 KB (with a WebSocket frame size of 32 KB), and others listed in the documentation covering Amazon API Gateway quotas and important notes.

- **Close code 1001** relates to these limits: API Gateway returns this status code when the client is idle for 10 minutes or reaches the maximum 2 hour connection lifetime.
- **Connection duration is a hard limit:** API gateway has a max connection duration of 2 hours on all websocket endpoints. This limit can't be increased. AWS's recommendation is that the client should recreate the connection when it detects that the connection is closed. Also, the server side should save messages in a database if currently there are no open connection to the client. For long-lived IoT-style connections, an AWS expert suggested IoT Core since it has a 24 hours connection limit and may be more appropriate for IoT use cases.
- **Oversized messages:** a user testing large payloads hit websockets.exceptions.ConnectionClosedError: code = 1009 (message too big), reason = Message too big. For larger payloads, consider sending a reference (e.g., an S3 URL) and letting the client fetch the full content.
- **Frames vs. messages:** one user testing the 32 KB frame vs. 128 KB payload distinction reported that they create a test web socket gateway and I send over it a packet composed exactly of 128Kbytes, and the communication was ok.

## Other relevant quotas

- There's a limit on how many new WebSocket connections you can open per second. By default, the limit is 500 connections per second (according to the documentation, this quota can be increased, although it's unclear to what extent)
- Throttle quota per account, per Region across HTTP APIs, REST APIs, WebSocket APIs, and WebSocket callback APIs | 10,000 requests per second (RPS) with an additional burst capacity provided by the token bucket algorithm, using a maximum bucket capacity of 5,000 requests. The burst quota is determined by the API Gateway service team based on the overall RPS quota for the account in the Region. It is not a quota that a customer can control or request changes to.
- Some regions have lower defaults: For the following Regions, the default throttle quota is 2500 RPS and the default burst quota is 1250 RPS: Africa (Cape Town), Europe (Milan), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Middle East (UAE), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Europe (Spain), Europe (Zurich), Israel (Tel Aviv), Canada West (Calgary), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Mexico (Central)
- Lambda integration timeout: the CLI example in the integration docs shows "TimeoutInMillis": 29000 as the default for a Lambda proxy (AWS_PROXY) integration.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:01:03.486Z

Mise is installed, your AWS config has a default profile in us-west-2, and git is set to your noreply address. I'm reading "lambda micro vms" as AWS Lambda. That one choice reshapes the coordinator, so it comes first.

## The Lambda fork

The handoff's coordinator is one long-lived process with in-memory maps and timers. Lambda keeps no memory between invocations and has no timers, so it cannot host that design as written. Two honest mappings exist on AWS.

**A. Serverless coordinator.** An API Gateway WebSocket API invokes Lambda on connect, disconnect, and every message. DynamoDB holds the ledger. Conditional writes make "claim this tile only if still pending" and "complete it only once" atomic, so single-assignment is enforced by the database instead of by a process. Pushes go out through the Management API. Consequences:

- **The clock is lazy.** Every invocation checks for expired heartbeats and blown straggler deadlines. Heartbeats arrive every second, so the clock ticks whenever anyone is alive. A once-a-minute EventBridge tick covers the idle case.
- **The job API is declarative.** Nothing can sit in an await across invocations. A job is a list of stages, each a pure function from the previous stage's results to a set of spawns, persisted in the ledger. Mandelbrot is one stage. Word count is map then reduce. Job code still has zero error handling.
- **Text frames only.** API Gateway disconnects clients that send binary frames with close code 1003. Pixels ride as base64 inside JSON, under 10KB per tile. Messages cap at 128KB and connections at two hours, so nodes reconnect on a timer. A reconnect is just churn, which the system already absorbs.
- **Concurrent writers.** Several Lambdas handle messages at once, so the ledger must stay correct under races. That is the real distributed-systems work here, and it is also the best part of the story. The coordinator has no memory, so a coordinator crash is a non-event too, and the handoff's single-point-of-failure caveat disappears.
- **Cost and latency.** Near zero on the free tier. A message round trip costs tens of milliseconds, which is fine against tiles that take a few hundred milliseconds with two tiles in flight per node.

**B. Always-on container.** The handoff's shape as written. One Node or Bun process on a t4g.nano or a Fargate task, with CloudFront in front for TLS. In-memory state, real timers, imperative await on spawned futures, binary frames. Roughly five to ten dollars a month. Simpler code, more operations surface, and the single point of failure stays.

I recommend A. It is more plumbing, but it turns the biggest caveat into the strongest claim, and you have said time is not the constraint.

## The stack, assuming A

**Tooling.** Everything installs through mise, and mise tasks replace Makefiles and npm scripts.

```toml
[tools]
node = "22"                 # matches the nodejs22.x Lambda runtime
bun = "1.3"                 # package manager, test runner, web bundler
aws-cli = "latest"
gh = "latest"
"npm:aws-cdk" = "latest"    # or opentofu / aws-sam-cli, your call below

[env]
AWS_PROFILE = "<the profile you pick>"
AWS_REGION = "us-west-2"

[tasks]
dev = "..."       # local coordinator on :3000 with live rebuild
test = "..."      # bun test, including the churn simulation
deploy = "..."    # cdk deploy, upload web to S3, invalidate CloudFront, print URLs
```

TypeScript everywhere. CDK's NodejsFunction bundles the Lambdas with esbuild. Bun bundles the browser code and runs the tests. Every tool above is in the mise registry except CDK, which comes through mise's npm backend.

**Repo layout.** A Bun workspace monorepo in a new `tabframe/` directory, its own git repo.

```
tabframe/
  mise.toml
  packages/
    protocol/          zod schemas for every message; the one source of truth for the wire
    core/              pure TS, no AWS, no DOM: Ledger, Scheduler, health model,
                       straggler speculation, result hashing, Job definitions
                       (Mandelbrot, WordCount); Store, Transport, Clock interfaces
    coordinator-local/ Bun.serve WebSocket + static files, in-memory Store, real timers
    coordinator-aws/   Lambda handlers ($connect, $disconnect, $default, tick),
                       DynamoStore with conditional writes, ApiGwTransport
    web/               host page (dashboard, controls, canvas, ledger view),
                       node.worker.ts (owns its socket, heartbeats, runs kernels),
                       kernels/mandelbrot.ts, kernels/wordcount.ts
    infra/             CDK: WebSocketApi, Lambdas, DynamoDB table, S3 + CloudFront
  docs/                decisions, architecture, rationale draft
```

The core is the same code locally and on AWS. Only Store, Transport, and Clock differ, so the churn simulation tests exercise the exact scheduler that runs in production.

**Ledger** as one DynamoDB table:

| Item | Holds |
|---|---|
| CONN#id | node or dashboard, owning nodeId, TTL |
| NODE#id | connection, lastSeen, health, tiles in flight, host tab |
| JOB#id | workload, current stage, parameters, counters, version |
| TASK#job#id | status, assigned nodes, attempts, deadline, result hash, result payload |
| META#sweep | last sweep time, so one invocation per second does the expiry pass |

Result payloads live in the task item, far below the item size cap. A dashboard that joins mid-frame gets a snapshot by querying the job partition, delivered in chunks under the message cap.

**Protocol**, JSON text frames:

| Direction | Messages |
|---|---|
| Node to coordinator | hello, heartbeat, result, ack |
| Coordinator to node | welcome, assign, cancel, command with close, freeze, or throttle |
| Dashboard to coordinator | subscribe, killHalf, freezeHalf, throttleHalf, restartFrame, selectWorkload |
| Coordinator to dashboard | snapshot, nodeJoined, nodeLeft, nodeHealth, taskAssigned, taskDone, taskReassigned, taskSpeculated, duplicateVerified, jobAdvanced |

Spawn is local. The host page starts more Web Workers. Kill, freeze, and throttle are cluster-wide commands routed through the coordinator, so they hit real tabs too. Throughput is computed on the dashboard from taskDone timestamps, which needs no server timer.

**Liveness and health.** Any inbound message refreshes lastSeen. Heartbeats every second, gone after four seconds of silence, and a socket close is gone immediately. The coordinator computes health from evidence rather than trusting the node. Fast or slow comes from tile durations against the cluster median. Throttled comes from the host tab reporting itself hidden. A tile past three times the median duration gets a speculative duplicate on another node. First result wins. The late duplicate is hashed and compared, and a match increments the verified counter on the dashboard.

**Determinism.** Kernels output integer iteration counts plus the final magnitude as a Float32, using only add, multiply, and compare on doubles. No log or exp inside the kernel, so two browsers on two machines produce bit-identical tiles and the hash comparison means something. Smooth coloring happens on the dashboard.

**Word count.** A bundled public-domain text split into chunks. Map tasks emit partial counts hashed into eight partitions. Reduce tasks merge one partition and return its top words. The dashboard shows the same ledger grid plus a growing top-words chart. Chunk sizes keep every reduce input under the message cap.

**Tests.** The core ships a seeded churn simulation. Virtual nodes join, die, freeze, and slow down at random while a frame renders. Assertions: every task done exactly once in the ledger, the assembled hash equals the single-node reference, nothing is ever assigned to a dead node, and speculation never yields a second accepted result. This is the evidence behind "still correct."

**What the reviewer gets.** A CloudFront URL for the page and an execute-api URL for the socket, both over TLS, no custom domain needed. One check belongs in M0: some AWS accounts carry a low default Lambda concurrency quota, and a render with many nodes would hit it. The first deploy step reads the account setting and requests a raise if needed.

Sources: [Binary media types for WebSocket APIs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/websocket-api-develop-binary-media-types.html), [Amazon API Gateway quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/limits.html), [WebSocket API overview and close codes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-websocket-api-overview.html).

Item 1: the runtime picture. Nothing here depends on the Lambda-versus-container choice; the coordinator is one logical endpoint either way.

```
 One browser tab = one HOST                              Server side
 +------------------------------------------+
 | Host page (main thread)                  |  HTTPS    +---------------------------+
 |  loads html + host.js + node.js  <-------+---------- | Static hosting            |
 |  dashboard: canvas, tile grid,           |           +---------------------------+
 |    node table, throughput, controls      |
 |  observer socket  <--------------------->+--- WSS -> +---------------------------+
 |  spawns node workers, relays visibility  |           | Coordinator               |
 |                                          |           |  ledger: nodes, jobs,     |
 |  +-------------+  +-------------+        |           |    tasks, results         |
 |  | Node worker |  | Node worker |  ...   |           |  scheduler                |
 |  | own socket  |  | own socket  |        |           |  liveness sweep           |
 |  | heartbeat   |  | heartbeat   |  <---->+--- WSS -> |  straggler speculation    |
 |  | kernels     |  | kernels     |        |           |  duplicate verification   |
 |  +-------------+  +-------------+        |           |  fan-out to observers     |
 +------------------------------------------+           +---------------------------+
  Every other tab, on any machine, is another host with its own observer and nodes.
```

**What happens when a reviewer opens the URL:**

1. **Page load.** The browser fetches the HTML and two bundles from static hosting. One bundle is the host page, the other is the node worker.
2. **Observer socket.** The host opens a WebSocket to the coordinator and subscribes. It receives a snapshot of the ledger plus the payloads of every tile already done, and paints them. From then on it receives a stream of events and draws each one.
3. **First node.** The host starts one Web Worker. The worker opens its own WebSocket, says hello, gets a node id, and posts that id back to the host for the "your nodes" panel. The coordinator assigns it up to two tasks. It computes in its own thread and sends results over its own socket. Results never pass through the host page.
4. **Fan-out.** On each result the coordinator stores it, marks the task done, assigns the node its next task, and pushes the tile to every observer in the cluster. Your tab and a stranger's tab paint the same pixel at the same moment.
5. **Heartbeat.** Each worker heartbeats every second on its own socket. The host relays visibility changes to its workers so a hidden tab reports itself as throttled.
6. **Controls.** Spawn is local: the host starts more workers, each a fully independent node. Kill half, freeze half, throttle half, and restart frame go over the observer socket to the coordinator. The coordinator picks victims across the whole cluster, including other people's tabs, and sends each victim a command on its own socket.
7. **Tab close.** Every worker in that tab dies at once, their sockets drop, the coordinator marks them gone, and their unfinished tasks go back to pending. No message is sent on the way out and none is needed.

**Properties this picture fixes in place:**

- **A node is one worker thread plus one socket.** A tab hosts one node by default and as many as you spawn. The coordinator never learns which tab a node lives in, and never needs to.
- **Two socket kinds.** Observers watch and send controls. Nodes work. A tab always has one observer socket and zero or more node sockets. An observe-only URL parameter gives a pure dashboard with no node.
- **One global machine, one continuous job.** Everyone joins the same job. When a frame completes the coordinator advances to the next preset location, so there is always work. With zero nodes connected, tasks simply wait as pending. The machine idles until a core shows up.
- **In-app spawn is bounded by the reviewer's CPU.** Ten workers in one tab share one machine's cores. The dashboard shows the core count and defaults spawn to cores minus one, and the rationale says so plainly. Real tabs on other machines scale for real.

Next is item 2, the node, when you're ready.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:12:10.208Z

One logical coordinator. That's the handoff's call and it stands: one WSS endpoint, one ledger, one scheduler, no consensus. What "one" means physically depends on item 6.

| | Always-on container | Serverless |
|---|---|---|
| Processes | Exactly one, long-lived | Many short-lived Lambda executions at once, none of them special |
| Where the state is | In that process's memory | In DynamoDB, which is itself replicated across three availability zones |
| What makes it "one" | Being a single process | Conditional writes, so two executions can never both claim the same tile |
| If it dies | Everything is lost, clients reconnect after restart, the job starts over | Nothing is lost, the next message runs on a fresh execution |

So in the serverless shape there is no coordinator process at all. The coordinator is the ledger plus a pure scheduling function, run by whichever execution happens to be handling a message. Dozens can be running simultaneously and the ledger stays consistent because the database arbitrates every claim.

That is also the honest way to say it in the rationale. The seed wanted a consensus-backed control plane. We don't build Raft, we rent a store that already runs it, and put only small metadata in it. That's the control-plane versus data-plane split from the seed, realized cheaply.

Nothing in our own design ever needs two coordinators. One global machine means one job, one ledger, one endpoint.

Yes, in the serverless shape. Each Lambda execution is one of those Firecracker microVMs you mentioned, and any number of them can be running the coordinator's logic at the same moment. None of them holds anything another would need.

The redundancy comes from splitting the coordinator into three parts that each live somewhere already redundant:

- **Connections** are held by API Gateway, a managed multi-AZ service, not by any execution.
- **State** is in DynamoDB, replicated across three availability zones.
- **Logic** is a pure function run by whichever execution picks up the message.

Kill any single machine in that path and nothing is lost. Two caveats keep the claim honest:

- **The executors don't agree with each other.** They never talk. Agreement is delegated to DynamoDB's conditional writes. That's simpler than Raft and it's rented, not built. The rationale should say so.
- **The container shape does not get this.** One process is one machine. Making it redundant means adding a load balancer and a shared store, at which point you've rebuilt the serverless shape with more moving parts.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:16:38.364Z

Item 2: the node. One Web Worker, one WebSocket, no DOM, no UI. Its bundle contains the protocol schemas, a socket client, and the two kernels. It is created by the host page and nothing else.

**Lifecycle, from boot to death:**

1. **Boot.** The host creates the worker and posts one init message: the coordinator URL, a host id for this tab, and the current visibility. The worker opens its socket.
2. **Hello.** On open, the worker sends hello with its host id and capabilities: core count and the kernels it carries. The coordinator answers welcome with a node id, the heartbeat interval, the in-flight limit, and a summary of the current job. The node never chooses its own id. The id is its address.
3. **Heartbeat.** Every second the worker sends a heartbeat carrying raw signals only: visible or hidden, queue length, last task duration, tasks done. It never labels itself fast or slow. The coordinator decides that from evidence.
4. **Assign.** The coordinator sends a task with an id, kind, input, attempt number, and deadline. The node keeps up to two in flight: one computing, one queued, so it never sits idle waiting for the next assignment to arrive.
5. **Compute.** The kernel runs in slices of about fifty milliseconds with a yield between slices. That yield is what lets the heartbeat timer fire and lets cancel and command messages get handled while a tile is mid-flight. Output is deterministic bytes.
6. **Result.** The worker sends the task id, attempt, the payload as base64, and the compute time. Then it starts the queued task and expects the coordinator to refill the queue.
7. **Cancel.** The coordinator can tell the node to drop a task, because a speculative twin finished first or the frame was restarted. The node drops it from the queue or aborts at the next slice boundary. A result already on the wire is harmless. The coordinator ignores or verifies it.
8. **Commands.** Fault injection arrives on this same socket, so it hits a node in any tab on any machine. Close means the worker ends itself and the socket drops. Freeze means it stops heartbeating and computing but keeps the socket open, which is the zombie the timeout path exists for. Throttle means it sleeps between slices and runs at a tenth of its speed while heartbeating normally. Resume undoes throttle.
9. **Death.** Tab closed, host called terminate, or a close command. All three look identical to the coordinator: the socket drops, nothing is sent first. The frozen zombie is the fourth case and is caught by silence. Once the coordinator declares a node gone it also closes the connection from its side, so a zombie never lingers.
10. **Reconnect.** If the socket drops while the worker is still alive, from a network blip or the two-hour gateway cap, the worker reconnects with backoff and says hello again. It becomes a brand new node. Whatever it had in flight was already released when the old node went silent.

**Host and worker talk through postMessage, and only about status.** The host sends init and visibility changes. The worker sends its node id and a state word: connecting, idle, busy, frozen, throttled, closed. Tasks and results never cross this boundary. The host panel that lists "your nodes" is built from these status posts alone.

**Choices worth calling out:**

- **A node is a connection.** No resume-my-old-identity logic. Every reconnect is a small churn event and the system already absorbs churn. This kills a whole class of stale-identity bugs.
- **No ack message.** The handoff had one. Liveness, results, and deadlines cover everything an ack would, and in the serverless shape every message is an invocation.
- **The node sends no hash.** The coordinator hashes payloads itself, so duplicate verification cannot be fooled by a node that lies about its hash. Free integrity.
- **The corpus never crosses the coordinator.** For word count, the text is a static asset next to the bundles. A map task's input is a byte range. The worker fetches the corpus once and slices it. Only reduce inputs, the partial counts, travel through the coordinator.
- **The node has no error path either.** A kernel that throws crashes the worker, the socket drops, and that is just a death. The only recovery logic in the entire system lives in the coordinator's reassignment.

Next is item 3, the coordinator's job.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:23:36.154Z

The short version: the node receives a description, not data, and returns bytes. A Mandelbrot tile is fully specified by a few numbers, so the input is about two hundred bytes of JSON and everything else is computed.

**Input: the assign message.**

```json
{
  "t": "assign",
  "taskId": "f42:t317",
  "attempt": 1,
  "kind": "mandelbrot",
  "deadlineMs": 4000,
  "input": {
    "frame": { "w": 2048, "h": 1280,
               "cx": -0.74364388703, "cy": 0.13182590421,
               "scale": 1.2e-9, "maxIter": 3000 },
    "tile":  { "x": 512, "y": 192, "w": 64, "h": 64 }
  }
}
```

The frame block is repeated in every assign rather than sent once in welcome. That makes a task computable from its input alone by any node with no prior context, which is exactly the property that makes reassignment trivial. It also means a frame restart can never leave a node holding stale view parameters.

**Compute.** For each pixel in the tile the kernel maps to the complex plane with the same formula everywhere, runs the escape loop, and records two things per pixel:

```
re = cx + (px - w/2 + 0.5) * scale
im = cy - (py - h/2 + 0.5) * scale
```

- **Iteration count** as a 16-bit integer. Interior pixels that never escape carry maxIter.
- **Escape fraction** as an 8-bit value for smooth coloring. It's found by binary search over 255 constant thresholds on the escape magnitude, so the kernel contains no log or exp, only add, multiply, and compare. Two browsers on two machines produce bit-identical bytes.

**Output: the result message.** The 64 by 64 tile yields 12KB of raw bytes, three per pixel. The worker deflates them, base64-encodes the result, and sends a text frame:

```json
{ "t": "result", "taskId": "f42:t317", "attempt": 1,
  "enc": "deflate+b64", "payload": "eJzt...", "computeMs": 143 }
```

Text frames because the gateway rejects binary ones. Deflate because iteration counts vary smoothly across most of a tile and compress well.

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Displayed frame | 1024 by 640 |
| Computed frame | 2048 by 1280, for antialiasing when drawn at half size |
| Tile | 64 by 64 computed, 640 tiles per frame |
| Raw payload per tile | 12KB |
| On the wire per tile | roughly 5 to 10KB, 16KB worst case |
| Per frame, per observer | about 5MB |

**Return path, three hops:**

1. **Node to coordinator.** The result goes over the node's own socket. The node keeps no copy and does no retry. If the socket dies mid-send the task is simply released when the node goes silent.
2. **Coordinator.** Decode, hash the bytes, and apply to the ledger. If the task is not yet done, mark it done and record the hash. If it is already done, compare hashes and count a verified duplicate or a mismatch. Then refill the node's queue and push a taskDone event with the payload inline to every observer.
3. **Observer to canvas.** Each host page inflates the payload, maps iteration plus fraction through a palette, and writes the pixels into the tile's rectangle on a full-size offscreen canvas. That canvas is drawn onto the visible one at half size, which gives the antialiasing for free.

Pacing is set per preset location: maxIter and zoom are chosen so one worker takes about a minute per frame. That leaves room to spawn and kill mid-render.

One thing this raises for item 3: where result bytes rest after the push. They can sit in the ledger item next to the hash, or in an object store with only the hash and a pointer in the ledger, which is the seed's control-plane versus data-plane split. The node doesn't care either way.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:27:17.436Z

Item 3: the coordinator's job. Shape-agnostic here; the one place the Lambda choice matters is flagged at the end.

**What it is.** A pure function over a ledger. Every input is an event: node hello, heartbeat, result, disconnect, observer subscribe, a control click, or a clock tick. The function takes the ledger and the event and returns the new ledger plus a list of effects, which are messages to send and connections to close. Nothing else has logic. That's what lets the same core run in a local process, in a Lambda execution, and inside a deterministic test with a fake clock.

**The ledger** holds five kinds of things:

| Record | Fields |
|---|---|
| Node | connection, host id, lastSeen, health label, visible flag, tasks in flight, rolling compute stats |
| Observer | connection, lastSeen |
| Job | kind, frame index, stage, parameters, counters for pending, done, reassigned, speculated, verified, mismatched |
| Task | job, kind, input, status of pending, assigned, or done, a list of attempts each with node, assignedAt, deadline, and outcome, then result hash and result ref |
| Meta | last sweep time, node cap, epoch |

Result bytes are not in the ledger. See below.

**Scheduling is one routine: fill a node.** Whenever a node has a free slot, from hello, from a result, or because another node died, the coordinator draws from three sources in strict priority:

1. **Released tasks.** Work that belonged to a node now gone. Oldest first, so churn never starves anything.
2. **Pending tasks.** Fresh work in the frame's tile order, center outward so the image grows from the middle.
3. **Overdue tasks.** Assigned work past its deadline with only one open attempt. Assigning one here creates a speculative twin on this node.

Speculation falls out of that third tier for free. A free slot only reaches tier three when tiers one and two are empty, which is exactly the end of a stage where stragglers hurt. Health does not gate assignment. Everyone gets work, a slow node just completes less of it, and the deadline is the safety net.

**Liveness.** Any inbound message from a node refreshes lastSeen. A sweep marks a node gone after four seconds of silence, or immediately on socket close. Going gone releases every open attempt the node had. A task whose only open attempt was on that node drops back to tier one. A task that also has a twin elsewhere stays assigned to the twin. Then the coordinator closes the connection from its side, so a frozen zombie never lingers, and emits nodeLeft and one taskReassigned per released task, which is what the dashboard flashes.

Observers ping every two seconds. That keeps the clock ticking when a reviewer freezes every node at once and there are no heartbeats left to trigger a sweep, and it keeps the gateway's ten-minute idle timer away.

**Deadlines.** Each attempt gets assignedAt plus three times the rolling median compute time, floored at a couple of seconds so nothing speculates during the first tiles when the median is unknown. A task never has more than two open attempts.

**Health labels** are computed by the coordinator from evidence, never asserted by the node. Fast or slow compares a node's rolling compute time to the cluster median. Throttled means the host tab reported itself hidden. Gone is silence. A label change emits a nodeHealth event.

**Results and verification.** On a result the coordinator hashes the bytes itself. If the task is not done, it becomes done with that hash, the node's slot is refilled, and a taskDone with the payload inline goes to every observer. If a twin is still running, it gets a cancel. If the task was already done, the hash is compared. A match counts as a verified duplicate, which is the live proof that recompute yields identical bytes. A mismatch is counted, shown in red, and the first result stands. Deterministic kernels mean that counter should read zero forever, and the rationale says untrusted hosts would need three-way voting instead.

An optional redundancy toggle opens two attempts on every task from the start, so every done tile earns a verified badge when its twin lands. It halves throughput and the toggle says so.

**Where result bytes rest.** Recommendation: a content-addressed object store, S3 in production and a map behind a local route in dev. The key is the hash. The ledger keeps hash plus key, about a hundred bytes per task. A new observer's snapshot is then the whole task table in one message, and it fetches done tiles by key over the CDN in parallel, cached, so ten observers joining cost one read. Live pushes still carry the payload inline for immediacy. This is the seed's control-plane versus data-plane split done literally, and it keeps every ledger write tiny.

**Observers and controls.** Subscribe returns the snapshot, then events stream. Throughput is computed on the dashboard from taskDone timestamps. Controls arrive on the observer socket. Kill, freeze, and throttle pick half the nodes at random across the whole cluster and send each a command, then emit controlApplied naming the victims so every dashboard animates the same ripple. Restart frame cancels all attempts and recreates the tiles. Next frame and select workload switch the job. Controls are rate limited per observer and the node cap is enforced at hello.

**Stage advance.** When the last task of a stage completes, the job definition yields the next stage's tasks, or the job ends. Mandelbrot ends a frame, pauses a few seconds so the finished image is seen, and advances to the next preset. Word count moves from map to reduce. That's item 4.

**Invariants, each one a test:**

- A task is done at most once. The first accepted result is final.
- Nothing is ever assigned to a node that is gone.
- Every task completes as long as one live node exists.
- At most two open attempts per task.
- Released work outranks fresh work.
- No correctness depends on a message from a dying node.

**Where the shape matters.** In a single process all of this runs serialized. With concurrent Lambda executions, each ledger transition becomes a conditional write: claim if still pending, complete if not done, increment in-flight if under the limit, sweep if nobody swept this second. A failed condition means another execution got there first, and the loser re-reads and continues. Same core, different store. Details in item 6.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:34:02.129Z

Two decisions recorded: the redundancy toggle is built in, and a mismatch discards everything and recomputes. Precisely: both results are thrown away, the task goes back to the front of the queue as contested, and it is done only when two fresh attempts agree. One consequence to be aware of: with the toggle off, a tile is painted on first result, so a later disagreeing duplicate would un-paint it and recompute. With the toggle on, a tile is painted only once two attempts agree, so nothing is ever retracted. Terminal rule so a broken kernel can't stall a frame forever: after two contested rounds the coordinator takes the majority hash across all attempts so far and marks the tile resolved by vote in red. Deterministic kernels mean none of this should ever fire, which is the point of showing the counter.

Now, where bytes rest. Three real options.

| | Ledger item | Content-addressed object store | Nowhere |
|---|---|---|---|
| Result bytes live in | the task record in DynamoDB | S3, key is the SHA-256 of the bytes | only the live push |
| Ledger holds | bytes and hash | hash only, the key is the hash | hash only |
| Late-joining observer | coordinator reads about 5MB and pushes it in some fifty chunks | one small snapshot of task states, then parallel fetches by hash over the CDN, cached | sees only tiles finished after it joined |
| Dedup and integrity | none | free, same bytes same key, observer can re-hash what it fetched | none |
| Extra infra | none | a bucket, a CloudFront origin path, one IAM grant | none |
| Per-frame cost | under a cent | under a cent | zero |

"Nowhere" fails the snapshot requirement, so it's out. Cost is a wash between the other two. The choice is architectural.

**I recommend the object store, for five reasons:**

- **It is the seed's split, literally.** The seed said hash equals name equals integrity equals dedup, with only the hash in the log. This is that sentence as infrastructure, and it's the cheapest thing in the build to point at in the rationale.
- **Ledger writes stay tiny.** Every task record is about a hundred bytes forever, whatever the tile size. Payload size stops being a ledger concern, which matters when word count's reduce inputs get bigger than a tile.
- **Snapshots scale with observers for free.** Ten people opening the dashboard cost S3 one read per tile. The CDN serves the rest. The coordinator never streams megabytes.
- **The dashboard can verify what it paints.** After fetching a tile by hash it re-hashes the bytes and compares to the ledger. If that ever fails the tile is drawn with a warning, not silently. End-to-end integrity for one line of code.
- **Completed frames are durable by accident.** A finished frame is a list of hashes. A gallery of everything the cluster has ever rendered is nearly free later, if wanted.

**Mechanics of a result under this design:**

1. The execution hashes the bytes and writes them to the store. Content addressing makes the write idempotent, so a twin's identical bytes are a no-op.
2. Then it does the conditional ledger update: complete if not done, else compare hashes.
3. Then it pushes taskDone to observers with the payload inline, so nobody waits on a fetch for live tiles.

If the execution dies between steps one and two, there's an orphan object and the task is still assigned. The deadline catches it. If it dies after step two, one push is missed. Events carry a sequence number, so an observer that sees a gap asks for a fresh snapshot and fills any holes by hash. Nothing depends on a push arriving.

A lifecycle rule expires objects after a few days so the bucket never grows unbounded. Mismatched results are stored too, under their own hashes, which makes a mismatch inspectable after the fact.

**Local parity.** The store is an interface with two methods: put bytes and return the hash, and give me the URL for a hash. In production that's S3 behind the CDN. In dev it's a map behind a route on the local server. The core never knows which.

Object store, unless you see a reason to keep bytes in the ledger.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:37:00.587Z

In order.

**1. What the ledger is.**

The ledger is the coordinator's memory. It is the one authoritative record of the machine's state: which nodes exist, what job is running, which task is in which state and who holds it, and for every finished task, the hash of the result we accepted. The test of what belongs in it: if the coordinator lost everything except the ledger, could it carry on correctly? Reassign what's unfinished, refuse to redo what's done, know which bytes are the real answer. Anything needed for that goes in. Anything else stays out.

It is current state, not a history of messages. Heartbeats don't get recorded, they update one timestamp. And it is not the pixels.

Where it physically lives follows the coordinator shape. In one long-lived process it's a handful of maps in memory. In Lambda it's a DynamoDB table, because an execution forgets everything the moment it returns, so every change has to be written out before the execution ends. The word "persist" is forced by Lambda, not chosen for durability. Durability is a side effect we then get to brag about.

**2. What we put in it.**

| Record | What's in it | Why it must be there | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, one per live node | id, connection id, host id, lastSeen, visible flag, rolling compute stats, the attempts it currently holds | connection id to reach it, lastSeen to detect death, attempts so we know what to release when it dies | ~300 bytes |
| Observer, one per dashboard | connection id, lastSeen | to fan events out | ~50 bytes |
| Job, exactly one | kind, frame parameters, stage, counters | so tasks can be composed into assign messages and progress computed | ~500 bytes |
| Task, one per tile | tile rect, status, list of attempts with node, assignedAt, deadline, outcome, and when done the accepted hash | this is the assignment ledger proper, and the hash is what makes a result authoritative | ~250 bytes |
| Meta, one | last sweep time, epoch, node cap | so concurrent executions don't all sweep at once | tiny |

A frame is 640 task records, so the whole ledger is around 200KB and every individual write is a few hundred bytes. Gone nodes are deleted, not kept.

What is deliberately not in it: result bytes, message history, anything an observer only needs for drawing. That's the seed's rule, small must-agree metadata in the control plane, bulk data out. It's also what keeps every update cheap, and in the serverless shape it's what makes conditional writes simple, because each record is small and independently updatable.

**3. How the object store helps.**

The problem it solves is only this: result bytes have to live somewhere so that an observer who joins mid-frame can see the tiles already finished. In a single process they'd sit in memory next to the ledger, and there'd be nothing to discuss. In Lambda there is no memory, so on every result the bytes must be written somewhere. Two candidates: inside the task record in DynamoDB, or in S3.

What putting them in S3 buys:

- **Two access patterns, two tools.** The ledger is hit with small conditional updates many times a second and read whole for snapshots. Bytes are written once, never updated, and read by many observers. DynamoDB is built for the first pattern. S3 behind a CDN is built for the second.
- **The coordinator never moves bulk data.** With bytes in DynamoDB, every observer join means the coordinator reads about 5MB and pushes it through the socket in some fifty chunks. With S3, the snapshot is the 200KB task table and the observer fetches the tiles it needs from the CDN in parallel, cached, so the tenth observer costs S3 nothing.
- **The key is the hash.** Store each result under its own SHA-256. Twin results from the redundancy toggle collide into one object. The ledger's "hash plus pointer" collapses to just the hash. An observer can re-hash what it fetched and refuse to paint a tile that doesn't match the ledger.
- **Ledger records stay small no matter the payload.** A tile is 12KB. A word-count reduce input can be much bigger. Neither ever touches a ledger write.

What it does not do: it is not a source of truth. An object with no ledger entry pointing at it is garbage, and a lifecycle rule expires it. The ledger says what is true. The store just holds the bytes the ledger names.

And in the single-process shape you'd skip S3 entirely. Bytes in a map, served from a route, same two-method interface: put bytes and get back a hash, give me a URL for a hash. The core never knows which one is behind it.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:43:23.910Z

It's the seed's design constraint number two and the heart of its Stage 5. Quoting the seed:

> **Strict control-plane/data-plane split.** Only small must-agree metadata reaches the consensus log; bulk data never does.

And Stage 5 spells out which side each thing falls on:

> **In the consensus log** (tiny, low-rate, must-agree): membership epoch, job/process table, capability & name registry, the **task-assignment ledger** (who owns what, what is committed done), and each completed result's **hash + pointer**.
>
> **Never in the log** (high-volume, recomputable): the actual compute, task inputs/outputs, inter-worker messages, heartbeats. Bulk result **bytes** live in a **content-addressed object store** replicated K-ways (hash = name = integrity = dedup); only the hash enters the log.

The reasoning behind it: agreement is expensive per byte and per operation, so you spend it only on facts that must be agreed on, and those are few and small. Bulk bytes don't need agreement. They're recomputable, and a hash in the log lets anyone check that the bytes they hold are the ones that were agreed. So bytes need availability, not consensus, and those are different jobs for different systems.

How it maps onto our build:

| Seed | Ours |
|---|---|
| The consensus log | The ledger. We don't run Raft, we rent DynamoDB, which is replicated and arbitrates with conditional writes |
| Membership epoch, job table, task-assignment ledger | Node records, the job record, task records with their attempts |
| Result hash plus pointer | Just the hash, since the object key is the hash |
| Content-addressed object store, K-way replicated | S3, which is already replicated, so we skip doing it ourselves |
| Heartbeats never in the log | Heartbeats only update one lastSeen field |
| Capability and name registry | Dropped, we have no user code or named endpoints |

When I said "the seed's rule" earlier, that's the sentence I meant: metadata in the ledger, bytes in the store, and only a hash bridging the two.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:47:30.245Z

Item 4: the job model. Two layers, and the line between them is the whole point.

**Kernels run on nodes.** A kernel is a pure function from an input to bytes. Same input, same bytes, on any machine. Three of them: `mandelbrot`, `wc-map`, `wc-reduce`, plus a one-task `wc-merge`. A node declares which kernels it carries in hello and gets assigned only those. Kernels know nothing about jobs, stages, or other tasks.

**Jobs run on the coordinator.** A job composes kernels into stages. A stage is a set of tasks that can run in any order on any node. When every task in a stage is done, a pure function of the results produces the next stage, or says the job is finished. That's the entire runtime API:

```ts
interface Job<P> {
  kind: string;
  start(params: P): Stage;                                   // first stage
  next(params: P, done: Stage, results: Results): Stage | null; // following stage, or finished
  then?(params: P): P | null;                                // what to run after this job
}
```

Look at what `next` receives: completed results only. There is no failed-task type anywhere in the API, no callback for a dead node, no retry count, no timeout parameter. A job author cannot write error handling because there is nothing to handle. Tasks complete. How many attempts that took, on which nodes, after which deaths, is invisible. That is the "user code has no error path" claim as a type signature.

**Mandelbrot is one stage.** The whole program:

```ts
export const MandelbrotFrame: Job<Frame> = {
  kind: 'mandelbrot',
  start: (frame) => stage('render',
    tilesCenterOut(frame).map(tile => task('mandelbrot', { frame, tile }))),
  next: () => null,
  then: (frame) => PRESETS[(frame.preset + 1) % PRESETS.length],
};
```

Every task input carries the full frame parameters and its tile, so a task is computable cold by any node. When the frame finishes, `then` hands back the next preset and the coordinator starts it after a short pause. That is the always-work loop.

**Word count is three stages, and that's why it's worth having.** Mandelbrot is embarrassingly parallel. Word count has dependencies between stages and data that has to move between them, which proves the job model is more than a tile scheduler.

```ts
export const WordCount: Job<Wc> = {
  kind: 'wordcount',
  start: (p) => stage('map',
    chunks(p.corpus, p.chunkBytes).map(c => task('wc-map', { corpus: p.corpus, ...c, R: p.R }))),
  next: (p, done, results) =>
      done.name === 'map'    ? stage('reduce', range(p.R).map(r =>
                                 task('wc-reduce', { r, maps: results.hashes() })))
    : done.name === 'reduce' ? stage('merge', [task('wc-merge', { parts: results.hashes(), topK: p.topK })])
    : null,
  then: (p) => ({ ...p, corpus: nextCorpus(p.corpus) }),
};
```

How the data moves:

1. **Map.** The corpus is a public-domain text shipped as a static asset. A map task's input is a byte range. The node fetches the corpus once, extends the range to the next whitespace on both ends so words are never split or double counted, tokenizes, and emits counts bucketed into R partitions by a fixed string hash. Output is one blob with a small header giving the offset of each partition's section. Around 150 tasks for a one-megabyte book.
2. **Reduce.** Task r's input is its partition number and the list of all map result hashes. The node fetches each map blob from the result store by hash, slices out section r, and merges. Bytes go from the store straight to the node. The coordinator passed hashes and never touched a word. Eight tasks.
3. **Merge.** One task takes the eight reduce hashes and produces a single top-K list. Since partitions hold disjoint words, the global top-K is exact. The dashboard renders that blob as a growing bar chart.

Tokenization rules, the partition hash, and output ordering are fixed and total, so map and reduce outputs are bit-identical across nodes and duplicate verification works for word count exactly as it does for tiles.

**What the coordinator does with a job.** Create means call `start`, mark its tasks pending, fill nodes. The last result of a stage means call `next`, and either mark the new tasks pending or mark the job finished and call `then`. The job record holds the current stage index and nothing else about progress, because the task records are the progress. Every step is a pure function, so a job can be stepped in a test with fake nodes running the real kernels. A single-node run yields the golden hashes, and the churn simulation must reproduce them exactly.

**The alternative I'm not recommending.** The seed's ABI is imperative: call spawn, get a future, await it. That reads nicely and works when the job lives in one long-running process. It cannot survive in anything that has no memory between steps without a replay mechanism, so choosing it here would decide item 6 by accident. The staged form gives the same no-error-path property, is shorter, and leaves item 6 open.

**On the dashboard** a job is a stage strip. For Mandelbrot the task grid is the image. For word count it's 150 squares, then 8, then 1, with the same colors for pending, assigned, reassigned, speculated, verified, and done, and the bar chart beside it.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T20:55:43.833Z

Closer than it looks, because of one property we already have: the scheduler, ledger, and job model never look inside a kernel. A kernel is an opaque pure function from input bytes to output bytes, and a job is a pure planner from results to the next stage. Nothing in items 1 through 4 changes if those two things arrive as user-supplied bytes instead of code compiled into our bundles. What is hardcoded today is only how the code gets to where it runs and who is allowed to write it.

## The gap, layer by layer

| Layer | What's missing today | What closes it | Distance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Code delivery | Kernels are baked into the node bundle | Store code in the same content-addressed store as results. A task names its kernel by code hash. Nodes fetch and cache by hash | Small, about half a day |
| Execution format and sandbox | Kernels are our trusted TypeScript | Kernel is a WebAssembly module with a fixed ABI: alloc, run, memory in and out. No imports at all, so no ambient authority. Each task runs in a disposable nested worker that's terminated at the deadline, which kills a spinning loop cleanly. Memory capped by the module | Small to medium, about a day |
| The planner | Jobs are TypeScript objects on the coordinator | The planner is also a WASM module, same sandbox, run by the coordinator. It gets params and stage results and returns the next stage spec. Node and Lambda both have a WASM runtime built in | Medium, about a day |
| Compile | Nothing | Three options below | Half a day to several days |
| Submission | No upload, one global job | Upload panel, validation of exports and imports, size caps, a FIFO job queue with the dashboard showing it | Medium, about a day |
| Consent and abuse | Nothing needed for trusted code | Lend-a-tab banner, per-job CPU budget, module caps, rate limits, kill switch | Small, but it's a policy surface |

The seed's fuller ABI, channels between running tasks and a mutable KV, I would leave out on purpose. Tasks that talk to each other mid-run are not restartable, and that restartability is the entire reason failure is a non-event. Staged, communication-free tasks are the design, not a shortcut. The seed's own constraint three, no mutable distributed state, points the same way.

## What "compile" could mean

- **Bring your own WASM.** The user uploads a module built with whatever they like: clang, Rust, Zig, Go, AssemblyScript. We run no compiler. The demo ships prebuilt example programs, Mandelbrot and word count among them. Honest, general, and nothing on the server to abuse. Smallest distance.
- **Compile in the browser.** AssemblyScript compiles TypeScript-like source to WASM entirely client-side in milliseconds. The submit box becomes "paste source." Real programs, no server compile, one library added to the page. Medium distance.
- **Compile on the server.** The seed's picture, C in, WASM out, via clang in a container. Real ops, slow cold starts, and an untrusted-input surface on the compiler itself. Largest distance and the least value per hour.

One bonus: WebAssembly is more deterministic than JavaScript for our purposes. Float arithmetic is IEEE with no fusion, and there is no engine-specific math library, so duplicate verification across browsers gets stronger, not weaker.

## The path I'd take

1. **Make the nodes a bare machine.** Content-addressed WASM kernels, fixed ABI, disposable sandbox worker, deadline kill. Reimplement Mandelbrot and word count as WASM modules and ship them as the demo programs. After this step the node bundle contains zero application code, and the rationale can say so.
2. **Make the planner a program too.** Same sandbox on the coordinator. Now a program is two modules, a planner for the control plane and a kernel for the nodes, in one ISA.
3. **Open the door.** Upload, validation, job queue, consent banner, budgets.
4. **Optionally, in-browser compile** with AssemblyScript so submitting a program means pasting source.

Roughly three to four days beyond the plan we've been walking through, with step one carrying most of the story value.

## What it changes in the sections so far

- **Item 2.** The node gains a kernel loader and a sandbox worker. Everything else stands.
- **Item 3.** The result store also holds code. The coordinator gains a job queue and runs planner modules.
- **Item 4.** The planner interface stays exactly as written. It just becomes an ABI instead of a TypeScript type.
- **Item 5.** Assign carries a code hash. An upload message appears.
- **Item 7.** Tooling grows a WASM toolchain for building the example programs, through mise.

The honest caveat for the rationale: WASM with no imports plus a disposable worker and a deadline is a real sandbox against what code can do. It does not protect against a host that lies, which is what redundancy and verification are for, and it does not hide the computation from the host, which the seed already rules out of scope.

This was the handoff's biggest cut, made to hold the eight-hour line. With that line gone it's the extension that turns "a fractal renderer with a good scheduler" into "a computer with an ISA."

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T21:00:35.011Z

Added back. Here is what "minimal but the capabilities are there" means concretely, then what it changes in the four items we've already walked.

## The program model

**A program is one WebAssembly module with two entry points and a manifest.**

- `plan` runs the control-plane side: given params, the stage index, and the previous stage's result hashes, it returns the next stage spec, or "done" with optional params for a follow-up job.
- `run` runs the core side: given a task's input bytes, it returns result bytes.
- The manifest is small JSON: name, default params, and a view, one of `tiles`, `bars`, or `text`, which tells the dashboard how to draw results.

Both entry points share one module, so a program is one file, and the module is stored content-addressed by hash like any other blob. A task names its program by hash. Nodes fetch, compile, and cache by hash.

**The ABI is bytes in, bytes out, and nothing else.** Exports: `memory`, `alloc`, `run`, `plan`. Imports allowed: only an abort stub. No fetch, no clock, no randomness, no host calls. A program can compute and that is all it can do. Upload validation checks exactly this list, plus a size cap and a declared memory maximum under a cap.

**Task inputs can name blobs.** A task input is inline bytes plus a list of store references, each a hash with an optional byte range. The host resolves them and hands the bytes to `run` alongside the input. That is how word count's map tasks get their slice of the corpus and how reduce tasks get map outputs, without the program ever having network access. A task can read exactly the blobs its planner named and nothing else, which is the seed's capability idea in miniature.

**The planner runs as a task on the machine.** When a stage finishes, the coordinator creates a plan task whose input is the params, the stage index, and the result hashes. Any node runs it in the same sandbox and returns the stage spec as a result. The coordinator validates the spec structurally, caps task count and size, and materializes the tasks. Consequences: the coordinator runs zero user code in any shape, planning is fault tolerant for free, every stage spec is a content-addressed and auditable blob, and the redundancy toggle verifies plans too. Cost is one extra task round trip per stage.

**Sandbox.** Each node runs tasks in a disposable sandbox worker separate from the worker that owns the socket. A task past its deadline is killed by terminating that worker, which stops a spinning loop cleanly, and a fresh one is spawned. The sandbox is reused across tasks of the same program otherwise, so compile and instantiate costs are paid once per program per node.

**Submission has two doors.** Drop a `.wasm` plus a manifest, or open the in-page editor, which is prefilled with the Mandelbrot source in AssemblyScript, edit it, and compile in the browser. The compiled module goes to the store by hash and a job is enqueued. The reviewer changes the coloring or the iteration count in the source and watches the cluster run their program, with nothing installed. That is the reason to include in-browser compile rather than bring-your-own-WASM alone.

**Jobs queue.** One job runs at a time. User-submitted jobs go ahead of automatic continuations, so a submission starts within seconds while the current frame is abandoned. The dashboard shows the queue and lets an operator skip or kill.

**Views.** `tiles` means the planner attaches a placement rectangle to each task and `run` returns RGBA pixels, which the dashboard blits. The program owns its own coloring, and since AssemblyScript's math compiles to WASM rather than calling the engine's library, that coloring is deterministic across browsers. `bars` means the final result decodes as label and value pairs. `text` means it's shown raw.

**Consent and budgets.** The page says plainly that an open tab lends CPU to programs other people submitted, sandboxed, with a stop-lending button. Per job: a task count cap and a total compute-seconds budget, after which the job is killed and marked over budget. Per program: size and memory caps. Per observer: a submission rate limit.

**The demo programs are real programs.** Mandelbrot and word count are written in AssemblyScript against a small SDK, compiled at build time, and shipped through the exact same store and queue as anything a user uploads. The node bundle contains no application code. Their source is what the editor opens.

## What changes in items 1 to 4

- **Item 1.** The page grows a programs panel, an editor, a queue view, and the consent banner. Nodes fetch modules from the store. Otherwise the picture stands.
- **Item 2.** A node becomes one socket, one orchestrating worker, and one disposable sandbox worker. The orchestrator fetches and caches modules by hash, resolves blob references, and runs tasks in the sandbox with deadline kill. Heartbeat, hello, commands, and death are unchanged.
- **Item 3.** The ledger gains a job queue and a program record per uploaded module. Plan tasks are ordinary tasks. The store holds code and data blobs as well as results, with an HTTP upload path since modules are too big for a socket message. Budgets are enforced at fill time. Nothing changes in scheduling, liveness, speculation, or verification.
- **Item 4.** The `Job` interface I wrote becomes the `plan` ABI, one to one. The three-byte tile encoding goes away in favor of RGBA from the program. Word count's corpus is uploaded to the store as a blob and referenced by range.

Five choices are baked into the above and are yours to veto: planner as a task rather than on the coordinator, in-browser compile included, programs return RGBA for tiles, blob references as the only data access, and one job at a time with user priority.

Item 5, the wire, is next and now includes the upload path and the assign format with program hash and blob references.

## Assistant · 2026-09-01T21:07:27.211Z

Aligned on the first part. The control plane runs no program code; it only manages executions. Adopting your word: one run of a program with params is an execution, and every task belongs to one. Then the second part, files, which is a real addition and I want to fit it in without breaking idempotency.

## Launching

1. **Upload.** The client puts the program's files into the store: the module, the manifest, and any input files such as a corpus. Everything content-addressed. A program bundle is literally a directory: a manifest mapping paths to blob hashes, itself stored as a blob. So a program is one hash.
2. **Launch.** The client tells the control plane: this bundle hash, these params, optionally inherit files from a previous execution. The control plane validates the module's imports and exports and the caps, creates an execution id, and queues it.
3. **Start.** When its turn comes, the control plane creates a plan task for stage zero and assigns it to a worker like any task. The worker runs `plan` in the sandbox and returns a stage spec.
4. **Run.** The control plane materializes the stage's tasks and fills nodes. Tasks run, read files, write files, return results. When the last one lands, a new plan task goes out for the next stage.
5. **Finish.** The planner eventually returns done, with optional params for a follow-up. The execution's final filesystem is recorded as one root hash. That's what a later execution can inherit, and what the gallery of finished frames is made of.

## Files

**The model: each execution has its own filesystem, versioned by stage, committed when a task completes.** A filesystem is a map from path to blob hash, stored as a blob, so the whole thing is one root hash on the execution record. A task sees the filesystem as of the start of its stage plus its own writes. Its writes become visible to the next stage, once the control plane accepts its result. Nothing is visible mid-task, and a task that dies wrote nothing.

That is what keeps the invariants intact. Re-running a task produces the same bytes and therefore the same hashes, so committing twice is a no-op, and with the redundancy toggle the twin's writes are verified against the first. Every path is written at most once per stage, so it is single-assignment under another name. Two tasks in one stage writing different bytes to the same path is a program bug, and the execution fails with that message rather than picking a winner.

**Results are files too.** The bytes `run` returns land at `/out/<stage>/<task>` automatically. The planner for the next stage reads them like anything else. The corpus for word count is `/in/corpus.txt`, uploaded with the bundle. The blob references I described last message go away; a task just reads by path.

**The ABI grows four imports, and that is the whole host surface:**

```
read(path, offset, len) -> bytes     // a range of a file as of stage start, or own writes
write(path, bytes)                   // buffered, committed with the result
list(prefix) -> entries              // paths and sizes under a prefix
log(bytes)                           // stdout, shown in the task detail on the dashboard
```

Plus the abort stub. Still no fetch, no clock, no randomness.

**How a read works inside the sandbox.** WebAssembly imports are synchronous, so the glue in the sandbox worker resolves the path against the stage's filesystem manifest, maps it to a hash, and fetches the bytes from the store with a synchronous request, which dedicated workers are allowed to make. Only paths in this execution's filesystem resolve, so a program cannot reach anything else. A per-node cache by hash makes repeat reads free, and the sandbox worker has nothing else to do while it waits, which is one more reason it is separate from the worker that heartbeats.

**How a write commits.** The glue buffers writes in memory. When `run` returns, the orchestrating worker hashes each written file, uploads the blobs to the store, and only then sends the result message with the list of path and hash pairs. The ledger never points at bytes that don't exist yet. When a stage completes, the control plane folds every task's writes plus the results into a new manifest and advances the root hash.

**Persistence across executions.** At launch, an execution starts from its bundle's files, optionally merged with the final filesystem of a named earlier execution, or the latest finished execution of the same program. The next Mandelbrot frame can read a cache the previous one wrote. Word count can accumulate. A program with `persist` in its manifest inherits latest by default. Everything is still write-once, because inheriting is just starting from a different root hash.

**Limits.** Per task, a cap on total bytes written and on the number of files. Per execution, a cap on total filesystem size. Reads cost a network round trip each, so the SDK documents reading whole files or large ranges, not thousands of tiny reads. Blob expiry after some days applies to everything, so old executions age out together, which is acceptable for a demo and stated.

## What this changes in what we've walked

- **Item 2.** The sandbox glue gains the four imports and the synchronous read path. The orchestrator gains the upload-then-report step for writes.
- **Item 3.** The ledger gains an execution record with a root hash and a queue position, and task records carry their writes. Stage completion now includes folding writes into a new root. The store gets an upload path used by nodes as well as by the launcher.
- **Item 4.** The planner reads previous results as files instead of receiving hashes. `run` may write as well as return.

Two choices in here you may want to override: synchronous reads through the glue rather than making the planner declare every file a task will read up front, and inherit-latest as the persistence default for programs that ask for it.
