Recorded as D13 through D15. Two consequences of those three decisions I want to lock before listing the rest, because they shape everything under them:

- **One image, two roles.** Control plane and cloud core are the same MicroVM image. The run-hook payload says which role to assume, so the snapshot is role-agnostic and there is one build. Cores use the no-ingress connector and connect outward through the same front door browsers use.
- **Cores must scale to zero when nobody is watching.** Two permanent cores would heartbeat forever, the control plane would never go idle, and both would run around the clock. So "two by default" means two whenever the machine is awake: the active control plane keeps two cores alive while any observer is connected or a human-launched execution is running, terminates them after ten idle minutes, pauses automatic continuation, and then suspends itself. The first visitor wakes it and the cores arrive within seconds.

Here is what's left, with the default I'd take on each. Say go, or name the ones to change.

## Item 6, the remaining pieces

| Question | Default |
|---|---|
| Authority while several control planes are in flight | Exactly one is active, stamped with a generation number. Others are booting or draining. "In flight" never means "authoritative." The alternative, several active control planes over a shared DynamoDB ledger, brings back conditional-write engineering for no demo value. The handover itself is the demo |
| Handover protocol | The fleet function launches the new control plane and waits for ready. It asks the old one to hand over: the old one stops assigning, pauses intake, serializes the ledger, and returns it. The new one adopts it, marks every node gone so their work is released, and becomes active. The fleet function flips the pointer, then tells the old one to drain: it closes every client with a reconnect code and is terminated after a grace period. Clients re-fetch a session and land on the new one. Cost under load is a few seconds of churn per hour |
| Failure paths | Old control plane unreachable: adopt from the latest S3 snapshot, a few seconds stale, which idempotency makes safe. Fleet function dies mid-rotation: the next run inspects both MicroVMs and finishes or rolls back |
| Who manages what | The fleet function manages control planes only. The active control plane manages cores: keeps two alive, replaces one that dies or nears its eight-hour ceiling, kills them on idle. Cores outlive control-plane rotations and simply reconnect |
| Front door | Two small Lambda functions sharing code. One vends sessions, endpoint plus thirty-minute token, on a public URL. One rotates, scheduled hourly, reserved concurrency of one so it is the single writer of the pointer, and it is also invoked by the session function when no control plane is running |
| Pointer store | An SSM parameter, since a single writer makes compare-and-swap unnecessary |
| Sizes | Control plane 1GB and half a vCPU for the 2MB/s bandwidth tier. Cores 0.5GB and a quarter vCPU, bursting to a full vCPU while computing |
| Idle policy | Control plane suspends after fifteen minutes without endpoint traffic, auto-resume on. Cores have no idle policy and a four-hour maximum duration as a cost fuse |
| Ledger snapshots | Every five seconds to S3 plus the suspend and terminate hooks, keyed by generation and time, kept for a day |
| Infrastructure code and account | CDK in TypeScript, default profile, us-west-2 |

## Amendments this forces on item 5

- A generation number on welcome, snapshot, and every message. A control plane rejects messages stamped with another generation.
- A dedicated close code meaning "rotating, reconnect now."
- Three internal endpoints on the control plane, handover, adopt, and drain, reachable only with a token the fleet function mints.
- One observer event, controlPlaneRotating, so the dashboard can show the generation, uptime, and a countdown to the next rotation. Watching the control plane roll over at the top of the hour while the render continues is worth a slot on the screen.

## Items 7 through 9

**Tooling and repo.** Bun for package management, tests, and browser bundles, Node 22 as the runtime target. AssemblyScript through npm. Workspace packages: protocol, core, control-plane, node-web, node-cloud, sandbox glue shared by both, the AssemblyScript SDK, the two demo programs, fleet, web, infra. Public repo carries the code plus a docs folder with the decisions, architecture, and rationale. No local ARM cross-build is needed, since Lambda builds the image from the Dockerfile itself.

**Tests and dev loop.** One local command starts the control plane, the local store, two local cores as Node processes standing in for MicroVMs, and the page. A second control plane process plus a script playing the fleet function tests handover on a laptop. The churn simulation, golden hashes from single-node runs, the real WASM programs under Node, sandbox tests for import validation, deadline kill, and memory caps, and schema tests for every message.

**Deploy and the reviewer's view.** A deploy is a new image version followed by a rotation, so deploys reuse the handover path. M0 verifies the six unknowns: WebSocket frames as idle traffic, sockets surviving token expiry, endpoint rate limits, the account memory quota, DNS inside the image, and resume latency at 1GB. Plus an AWS budget alarm, and a page state for the first visitor that says the machine is waking and shows cores arriving.

Synchronous file reads through the glue rather than declared prefetch. Programs marked persist inherit the latest finished execution. Tile results are RGBA written by the program. Blobs expire after seven days. No operator token, all controls public. Heartbeat every second, gone after four. Frame 1024 by 640 displayed, tiles 64 pixels computed. ## 6. Hosting and fleet (settled)

**Platform:** AWS Lambda MicroVMs, us-west-2, default profile. Facts that shape the design: snapshot-booted Firecracker VMs; dedicated TLS endpoint per MicroVM with WebSockets; every request needs a JWE token (1–60 min) — browsers pass it as WebSocket subprotocols / a fetch header; **8-hour hard maximum** (running + suspended); idle policy suspends on no endpoint traffic and auto-resumes; endpoint bandwidth capped by size (1 MB/s at 0.5 GB, 2 MB/s at 1 GB) → **bytes never transit the control plane**; ARM64; CFN/CDK for images, API for running instances.

**Topology:**
- **Fleet functions** (two Lambdas sharing code): `session` on a public URL vends `{endpoint, token(30 min), expiry}` and triggers a heal when no control plane is running; `rotate` runs hourly on EventBridge with reserved concurrency 1 and is the **sole writer** of the pointer.
- **Pointer:** one SSM parameter naming the active control-plane MicroVM and generation.
- **Control plane:** one Node process in a MicroVM (1 GB / 0.5 vCPU), idle policy suspend after 15 min, auto-resume on, max duration 8 h (rotated hourly anyway).
- **Cloud cores:** two MicroVMs (0.5 GB / 0.25 vCPU, burst to 1 vCPU), `NO_INGRESS`, no idle policy, 4 h max duration as a cost fuse; they fetch a session and connect outward like a tab.
- **Store:** S3 behind CloudFront (`GET /blob/<hash>`), presigned hash-pinned PUTs minted by the control plane. **Static assets** on CloudFront.
- **One image, two roles:** control plane and core are the same MicroVM image; the run-hook payload selects the role, so the snapshot is role-agnostic.

**Authority:** exactly one control plane is *active*, stamped with a **generation**. Others are booting or draining. Every message carries the generation; a control plane rejects foreign generations.

**Hourly handover (also the deploy path):** `rotate` launches CP(g+1) and waits for ready → asks CP(g) to hand over (stop assigning, pause intake, serialize ledger, return it) → posts it to CP(g+1) `/adopt` (marks every node gone → work released; becomes active) → flips the pointer → tells CP(g) to `/drain` (close every client with the *rotating, reconnect* code) → terminates CP(g) after a grace period. Clients re-fetch a session and reconnect. Under load: a few seconds of churn per hour. **Fallbacks:** CP(g) unreachable → adopt the latest S3 snapshot (≤5 s stale; idempotency makes it safe). `rotate` dies mid-way → next run inspects both MicroVMs and finishes or rolls back.

**Core management:** the active control plane keeps two cores alive while any observer is connected or a human-launched execution is running; replaces a core that dies or nears its ceiling; after 10 idle minutes terminates cores and pauses automatic continuation, after which the control plane itself suspends. Cores outlive control-plane rotations and simply reconnect.

**Snapshots:** ledger to S3 every 5 s plus the suspend and terminate hooks, keyed by generation and time, kept one day.

**Item 5 amendments:** generation on welcome/snapshot/every message; close code *rotating, reconnect now*; internal `/handover`, `/adopt`, `/drain` endpoints on the control plane, token-gated to the fleet function; observer event `controlPlaneRotating {gen, next}` for a dashboard banner with uptime and countdown.

**M0 verifications (docs are silent):** WebSocket frames count as idle-policy traffic; an open socket survives its token's expiry; endpoint 429 thresholds; account MicroVM memory quota; DNS inside the image (third party reports UDP egress blocked); resume latency at 1 GB.

**Cost:** idle ≈ $0.08/month (snapshot storage); reviewer hour ≈ $0.13 (control plane + two cores); left running all day ≈ $3.

**Small defaults, confirmed:** synchronous file reads through the glue; `persist` programs inherit latest; tiles are RGBA from the program; blobs expire after 7 days; no operator token; heartbeat 1 s / gone at 4 s; frame 1024×640 displayed, 64-px computed tiles; one public-domain book as corpus.

---
'''

s = s.replace('\n## 6. Rationale hooks captured so far', hosting + '\n## 7. Rationale hooks captured so far', 1)

Here's what I found about running the AssemblyScript compiler in the browser via `web.js`.

## Official documentation (assemblyscript.org)

The most relevant result is the official "Using the compiler" page. The compiler runs in browsers as well. The simplest way to set it up is to include the generated web.js so the compiler can be used with an import on the Web, after which you can write `import asc from "assemblyscript/asc";` in a module script. The docs note that x.x.x must be replaced with the respective version to use, or latest to always use the latest version (not recommended in production).

**How web.js works:** By default, the script installs the necessary import map and, for browsers that do not yet support import maps, an import map shim. It also accepts the following options in case there is a need to only perform part of the setup:

| Script URL | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `web.js?noinstall` | Does not install the import map. |
| `web.js?noshim` | Does not install the import map shim. |
| `web.js?noinstall,noshim` | Does not install the import map or shim. |

Regardless of the options used, the script always declares the following global variables (the page was truncated before listing them — see the link for details).

**Programmatic API:** The same page shows the compiler API that works in both Node and the browser — `asc.main([...])` accepts command-line-style options plus API hooks such as `stdout`, `stderr`, `readFile`, `writeFile`, `listFiles`, `reportDiagnostic`, and `transforms`, returning `{ error, stdout, stderr, stats }`. In the browser, you'd typically supply `readFile`/`writeFile` callbacks so the compiler can work against in-memory sources instead of a filesystem.

## Historical context

Older forks of the repo show that a browser build has existed for a long time, though under a different name. In early versions, to build an UMD bundle to dist/assemblyscript.js (depends on binaryen.js): `npm run build`. This also builds a browser version of asc to dist/asc.js (depends on assemblyscript.js). The modern `web.js` import-map approach replaced that older `dist/asc.js` UMD bundle.

Related background: portable compiler sources compile to both JavaScript using tsc and WebAssembly using asc, and the project notes that this builds the compiler as a library, while the asc frontend setting it up and feeding it source files is JavaScript for now.

## Other results

The remaining results were less relevant — a general Wikipedia entry (noting the stable release: 0.28.9 / 18 October 2025), an unrelated ActionScript-to-JS compiler, and an AssemblyScript project template that shows browser/Node/WASI build targets but not the in-browser compiler itself.

For the full setup snippet and the list of globals that `web.js` declares, the source to check is https://www.assemblyscript.org/compiler.html.

Yes — the `nodejs22` package is available in the Amazon Linux 2023 repositories and can be installed with `dnf`. Here's a summary of what the search turned up:

**Package availability confirmed**

The official AL2023 documentation shows `nodejs22` as a native RPM package. In its TypeScript guide, AWS demonstrates installing it directly: Install a TypeScript compiler for Node.js 20 and 22 — Node.js 20 and 22 will be installed automatically: `$ sudo dnf install -qy nodejs20-typescript nodejs22-typescript`, with the resulting installed package shown as nodejs22-22.19.0-1.amzn2023.0.1.x86_64. The docs also note that this is precisely how RPM packages available on Amazon Linux, such as nodejs20-typescript or nodejs22-typescript, install a TS compiler: globally at the system level, and separately for each supported Node.js version.

Security advisories also confirm the package is actively maintained. A Tenable plugin for advisory ALAS2023-2026-1465 covers Amazon Linux 2023 : nodejs22, nodejs22-devel, nodejs22-full-i18n and recommends: Run 'dnf update nodejs22 --releasever 2023.10.20260302' or 'dnf update --advisory ALAS2023-2026-1465 --releasever 2023.10.20260302' to update your system.

**How to install**

```bash
sudo dnf install -y nodejs22
```

**Multiple versions side by side**

AL2023 uses the `alternatives` system so multiple Node.js versions can coexist. After installing both 20 and 22, the docs show link currently points to /usr/bin/node-20 ... /usr/bin/node-22 - priority 100, slave npm: /usr/bin/npm-22, slave npx: /usr/bin/npx-22. If Node 22 isn't the active default, you can switch with `sudo alternatives --set node /usr/bin/node-22`, or call `node-22` / `npm-22` directly.

**Background / history**

- The package originated from a community request: In October 2024 Node.js 22 moved to LTS. https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v22.11.0 ... This is an upgrade of (but not replacement of to maintain backwards compatibility) nodejs20.
- Note that the plain `nodejs` package is older — one bug report stated the package nodejs.x86_64 is version 1:18.20.4-1.amzn2023.0.1. This needs to be updated to NodeJS 22, or at least NodeJS 20. So be sure to install `nodejs22` specifically rather than `nodejs`.
- A follow-up request for `nodejs24` has been filed, with the expectation to be able to install multiple nodejs versions on a running system (18, 20, 22, 24).

**Related: Lambda**

If you're working with Lambda, the Node.js 22 runtime is based on the provided.al2023 runtime, which is based on the Amazon Linux 2023 minimal container image. The Amazon Linux 2023 minimal image uses microdnf as a package manager, symlinked as dnf.

Here's what I found about the `AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage` CloudFormation resource and its CDK counterpart:

## Background: Lambda MicroVMs

This is a fairly new AWS capability (launched roughly 2–3 months ago). A MicroVM image is a resource that defines the filesystem and application environment of a MicroVM. The MicroVM image includes your runtime environment, application code, and supporting programs such as background processes and observability agents. To create a MicroVM image, you provide a zip package that contains a Dockerfile and your application artifacts, which you upload to Amazon S3. During the build, Lambda retrieved the zip, ran the Dockerfile, initialized the application, and took a Firecracker snapshot of the running disk and memory state. Build logs streamed in real time to Amazon CloudWatch under /aws/lambda/microvms/, and when the image was ready it appeared in the console with its Amazon Resource Name (ARN) and version number.

## CloudFormation / CDK support

Lambda MicroVMs launched with full AWS CloudFormation and AWS CDK support. The AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage resource type manages the image build lifecycle through the stack. Running MicroVMs (the per-user ephemeral instances) are still API/SDK-managed since they're dynamic runtime resources, not static infrastructure.

A community blog post shows the resource's property surface in a CloudFormation template — key properties include `Name`, `Description`, `BaseImageArn` (e.g. `arn:aws:lambda:${Region}:aws:microvm-image:al2023-1`), `BaseImageVersion`, `BuildRoleArn`, `CodeArtifact.Uri` (an S3 URI to the zip), `AdditionalOsCapabilities`, `CpuConfigurations` (with `Architecture`), `Resources` (with `MinimumMemoryInMiB`), `EgressNetworkConnectors`, `EnvironmentVariables`, `Hooks`, and `Logging.CloudWatch`. One gotcha noted: the BaseImageVersion property is required but the correct value isn't obvious. You need to query it via the `aws lambda-microvms` CLI.

In CDK, the L1 construct is `CfnMicrovmImage` in the `aws_lambda` module (following the standard `Cfn*` naming convention for auto-generated L1s). I wasn't able to surface the dedicated CDK API reference page for it in the search results, but there's a related `AWS::Lambda::NetworkConnector` L1 as well.

## Community L2-style construct

There's a Python construct wrapping the L1: LambdaMicroVM is a typed wrapper around the L1 AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage resource. In one construct it zips your Dockerfile+app, uploads it to S3, creates least-privilege build and VM-execution roles, resolves the managed base-image version, and emits a snapshotted MicroVM image — with secure defaults and an overrides escape hatch for anything not yet modeled. It's on PyPI as `lambda-microvm-cdk` and on GitHub at `ran-isenberg/lambda-microvm-cdk-python`. The design separates images and connectors (declarative CDK); the running instance is runtime-only, wired from the construct's outputs.

## Related: CloudTrail

Note that the same resource type name is used for CloudTrail: the CloudTrail resource type for Lambda MicroVMs data events is AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage.

## Useful links
- AWS Docs – MicroVM images: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/microvms-images.html
- AWS Docs – Getting started: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/microvms-getting-started.html
- AWS News Blog launch post: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/run-isolated-sandboxes-with-full-lifecycle-control-aws-lambda-introduces-microvms/
- Community CDK construct: https://github.com/ran-isenberg/lambda-microvm-cdk-python
- Blog with CFN template + CDK example: https://dev.to/aws-builders/i-made-an-aws-lambda-microvm-publicly-accessible-for-0month-heres-the-full-setup-36fn

Three facts I verified for item 7 before writing it: Node 22.23 on this machine runs TypeScript files directly with no flags, so the control plane needs no build step to run locally. The AssemblyScript compiler runs in the browser through its `web.js` import-map setup with in-memory read and write callbacks, so the editor and the build use the same compiler. And CDK has the L1 `CfnMicrovmImage` for `AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage`, plus `nodejs22` is a stock Amazon Linux 2023 package, so the image is a plain Dockerfile.

## Item 7: tooling and repo

**Runtimes.** Node 22 is the production runtime everywhere: in the MicroVM image, in the two fleet Lambdas, and for CDK. Bun is the developer toolchain: package manager with workspaces, test runner, and bundler for the browser bundles. Nothing at runtime depends on Bun, so the local process and the MicroVM process are the same code on the same runtime.

**mise.toml**, the whole tool story:

```toml
[tools]
node = "22"
bun = "1.3"
aws-cli = "latest"
gh = "latest"
"npm:aws-cdk" = "latest"

[env]
AWS_PROFILE = "default"
AWS_REGION = "us-west-2"
_.file = ".env.local"        # gitignored per-machine overrides

[tasks.install]  run = "bun install"
[tasks.dev]      run = "node packages/dev/src/up.ts"        # control plane + local store + 2 local cores + web, rebuilding
[tasks.test]     run = "bun test"
[tasks.build]    depends = ["build:programs", "build:web", "build:image"]
[tasks."build:programs"] run = "node packages/sdk-as/scripts/build-programs.ts"   # asc → programs/*/dist
[tasks."build:web"]      run = "bun build packages/web/src/{host,node,sandbox,editor}.ts --target=browser --outdir packages/web/dist"
[tasks."build:image"]    run = "bun build packages/control-plane/src/main.ts --target=node --outfile packages/control-plane/dist/main.js"
[tasks.deploy]   depends = ["build", "test"]; run = ["cdk deploy --all", "node packages/infra/scripts/image.ts", "node packages/fleet/scripts/rotate.ts"]
[tasks.verify]   run = "node packages/infra/scripts/verify-m0.ts"                  # the six MicroVM unknowns
[tasks.logs]     run = "aws logs tail /aws/lambda/microvms/tabframe --follow"
```

AssemblyScript is deliberately not a mise tool. It is a workspace devDependency, so the build-time compiler and the in-browser compiler are pinned to one version, and a program the reviewer edits compiles exactly like the one we shipped.

**Layout**, a Bun workspace:

```
tabframe/
  mise.toml  package.json  tsconfig.base.json  biome.json
  packages/
    protocol/        zod schemas + types for every message, close codes, generation, limits; canonical codecs
    core/            pure control-plane logic and the churn simulation harness; Store/Transport/Clock interfaces
    control-plane/   the process: http + ws, lifecycle hooks, handover/adopt/drain, presign, S3 snapshotter,
                     core fleet manager, local store route; Dockerfile
    sandbox/         WASM glue: ABI, the five imports, FS manifest resolution, caps;
                     adapters: web worker (sync XHR) and node worker_thread (Atomics.wait)
    node/            the orchestrator; entry points platform/web.ts and platform/node.ts
    web/             host page, dashboard, controls, editor, programs panel, queue, banners
    sdk-as/          AssemblyScript SDK and the program build script
    fleet/           the two Lambdas: session and rotate, sharing a lambda-microvms client and the SSM pointer
    infra/           CDK app and the image publish script
    dev/             the one-command local topology
  programs/
    mandelbrot/      assembly/index.ts, manifest.json
    wordcount/       assembly/index.ts, manifest.json, in/corpus.txt
  docs/              decisions, architecture, rationale
```

One `node` package with two platform entry points rather than two packages, because the orchestrator logic is identical and only the worker primitive and the synchronous read path differ. Same for the sandbox.

**The image.** One Dockerfile, both roles:

```dockerfile
FROM public.ecr.aws/lambda/microvms:al2023-minimal
RUN dnf install -y nodejs22 && dnf clean all
COPY packages/control-plane/dist/main.js /app/main.js
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "/app/main.js"]
```

The process reads its role from the run-hook payload, so the snapshot is role-agnostic. Bundling to a single file keeps the snapshot small, which is what resume latency is made of. Lambda builds the image on ARM64 itself, so no local cross-build and Docker stays optional for parity checks.

**CDK.** `CfnMicrovmImage` for the image, with the required base image version looked up once by the publish script since it is not obvious from the console. Roles: a build role that reads the artifact bucket, an execution role that can presign and write the blob and snapshot buckets, read the SSM pointer, and run and terminate core MicroVMs. Two `NodejsFunction`s for the fleet, one with a function URL and one on an hourly EventBridge rule with reserved concurrency of one. Buckets for artifacts, blobs, snapshots, and web. One CloudFront distribution with two origins. An SSM parameter. A budget alarm. CDK outputs write the front-door URL and store base into the web bundle's config file at deploy time.

**Deploy is a rotation.** `mise run deploy` synthesizes the stack, publishes a new image version, and invokes rotate, which launches a control plane from the new version and hands over. Rolling deploys fall out of the design for free.

**Repo.** Public GitHub repo named `tabframe`, created with `gh` at M0 after you log in with `! gh auth login`. Commits under your existing noreply identity, so no email leaks. Main branch only, small commits. Code plus the docs folder, seed and handoff kept out. Transcripts exported per session into `docs/transcripts/` since they are a deliverable.

**Lint and format.** Biome, one devDependency, one config.

Item 8, tests and the dev loop, is next.

Sources: [AssemblyScript compiler usage](https://www.assemblyscript.org/compiler.html), [MicroVM images](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/microvms-images.html), [community CDK construct](https://github.com/ran-isenberg/lambda-microvm-cdk-python), [AL2023 TypeScript and nodejs22](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/linux/al2023/ug/typescript.html).

## Assistant · 2026-09-02T01:48:52.094Z

Acknowledged and recorded: you create the repo, and it stays private until the end. Item 8, tests and the dev loop.

## The dev loop

`mise run dev` brings up the whole machine on the laptop with one command:

- **The control plane** as a Node process running TypeScript directly under `node --watch`, in local mode: in-memory ledger, the store as a local route with a hash-verifying PUT, presign returning URLs to itself, and the session endpoint emulated so the page gets a localhost endpoint and a dummy token. The lifecycle hooks are ordinary routes, so a dev script can POST run, suspend, resume, or terminate to exercise them.
- **Two local cores** as Node processes running the node platform entry point against the local control plane. They stand in for the MicroVM cores and keep the Node adapter of the sandbox exercised every day, not just at deploy.
- **The web bundles** rebuilt on change by Bun in watch mode and served by the control plane. Open one URL, you are a node, and the two local cores are already there.
- **Seeding**, which is the same code the production control plane runs on first boot: compile the demo programs, put their bundles in the store, queue the Mandelbrot continuation.

`mise run dev:rotate` starts a second control plane on another port and drives the real rotate code with a local driver against both. You watch the banner, the reconnect, and the released tiles on the dashboard. Handover is testable on a laptop before it ever touches AWS.

## Test layers

| Layer | What it proves | Runner |
|---|---|---|
| Protocol | Every schema round-trips, invalid and oversized messages are rejected, generation stamping is enforced | bun test |
| Core, pure | Fill priority, liveness, deadline math, health labels, both verification policies, stage fold and conflict detection, queue ordering, snapshot round-trip, adopt marks all nodes gone, desired-core policy | bun test |
| Churn simulation | Correctness under arbitrary churn. Detailed below | bun test, seeds in a matrix |
| Sandbox | Forbidden imports rejected, missing exports rejected, memory cap enforced, an infinite loop is killed at the deadline, write caps, unresolvable paths error, traps captured, no state leaks between tasks, same input gives same bytes | bun test on the Node adapter; Playwright for the web adapter's synchronous read path |
| Programs | Both demo programs compile, tile hashes match goldens, word count matches a plain JavaScript count of the corpus, plan outputs validate against the stage-spec schema | bun test |
| Control plane process | Real sockets against a spawned process: hello to result, presign then PUT then hash check, role selection from the run payload, snapshot written on suspend, handover between two processes, drain close code, foreign generation rejected | bun test |
| Fleet | Rotate and session logic against a fake MicroVM client: launch, wait, handover, flip, drain, terminate, and the failure branches, old control plane unreachable and crash mid-rotation | bun test |
| Browser end to end | The reviewer's path, automated. Below | Playwright, Chromium |
| Infra | Stack synthesizes, and `cdk diff` runs before every deploy | bun test |

## The two that carry the submission

**The churn simulation** is the evidence behind "still correct." A seeded generator drives N virtual nodes through random join, leave, freeze, throttle, and kill events against the real core, with a virtual clock and a fake store, running the real WASM programs under Node. Invariants are asserted after every event, not just at the end: a task is done at most once, nothing is assigned to a gone node, at most two open attempts, released work outranks fresh work, no step depends on a message from a dying node. At the end, every output hash must equal the golden from a single-node reference run. Two extra scenarios: a lying node that returns corrupt bytes, which must produce a mismatch, a recompute, and the correct final image, and the redundancy toggle on, where no tile may be accepted without agreement. A few seeds run by default, thousands in the long mode, and any failure is replayable from its seed.

**The Playwright run** is the money shot as a test. Open the page, wait for the local cores and the tab's node to appear, spawn ten, kill half, wait for the frame to complete, hash the canvas, compare to the golden. A second run pastes a modified Mandelbrot source into the editor, compiles in the browser, launches, and checks the result. A third performs a local rotation mid-render and asserts the frame still completes with the right hash.

**Goldens** come from `mise run goldens`, a single-node run of each demo program at fixed params, committed next to the program. Anything that changes a kernel changes its golden on purpose, in the same commit.

**Determinism plumbing** that makes all of this possible: the core takes an injected clock and an injected random source, so simulation time is virtual and victim selection for kill-half is replayable. Fixtures for the sandbox tests, an infinite loop, a memory hog, a trapping module, a module with a forbidden import, are tiny AssemblyScript sources compiled at test time by the same pinned compiler.

**Runners and CI.** `mise run test` runs bun test then Playwright. A minimal GitHub Actions workflow on the private repo runs install, lint, and both suites on every push. No AWS credentials exist in CI. Deploys are manual from the laptop, and `mise run verify` is the M0 runbook against the real account, not a test.

Item 9, deploy and the reviewer's view, is next.

## Assistant · 2026-09-02T01:52:55.646Z

Recorded item 8. Item 9, deploy and the reviewer's view.

## M0: first deploy and the six verifications

The first deploy is deliberately a skeleton: buckets, CloudFront, the two fleet functions, the SSM pointer, and an image whose control plane only does hello and heartbeat. Its job is to retire the unknowns before any real logic exists. Order: you create the repo and log in with `! gh auth login`, I confirm the AWS identity, run `cdk bootstrap` once, deploy, publish the image, invoke rotate to start the first control plane, hit the session URL, open a socket. Then `mise run verify`:

| Unknown | How we check | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| WebSocket frames count as idle-policy traffic | Connect, send frames past the idle window, read the MicroVM state | Observer pings become small HTTP requests to the endpoint instead of socket frames |
| An open socket survives its token's expiry | Mint a one-minute token, connect, wait two minutes, check the socket | Sixty-minute tokens and clients reconnect at fifty-five |
| Endpoint rate limits behind the 429 | Ramp request rate until throttled, record the number | Coalesce events per observer and lower heartbeat rate |
| Account MicroVM memory quota | Read Service Quotas | Request an increase on day one, since three MicroVMs need about 2GB |
| DNS and S3 reachability inside the image | A diagnostics route in the control plane resolves a name and HEADs a bucket | VPC egress connector with its own DNS, or IP endpoints |
| Resume latency at 1GB | Suspend by API, time the first request | Smaller baseline, or keep the control plane warm with a scheduled ping |

Results go in `docs/m0-verification.md` with the design adjustments, if any. Nothing past M0 is built on an assumption the docs left open.

## Deploy, rollback, and guards

**A deploy is a rotation.** `mise run deploy` builds, tests, synthesizes and applies the stack with the web assets, publishes a new image version and waits for it to go active, then invokes rotate. The new control plane comes up on the new version, adopts the ledger, and the old one drains. Cores are replaced on the new version by the fleet policy over the next cycle. Web assets use hashed filenames with a short TTL on the index, and a protocol version bump makes stale pages reload once.

**Rollback** is a rotation to the previous image version, which is immutable, plus deactivating the bad one. Web assets roll back by redeploying the previous build.

**Observability in production:** MicroVM logs in CloudWatch under the image's log group, fleet function logs, a health route and the diagnostics route on the control plane, and the dashboard itself showing generation, uptime, and the countdown to the next rotation.

**Cost guards, all of them:** idle policy on the control plane, no cores and no continuation without an observer, maximum durations on every MicroVM, the node cap, blob expiry, and an AWS Budgets alarm at a monthly ceiling you pick. The alarm needs a notification address, and I will not put yours anywhere without you naming it. Plus a kill switch: `mise run down` terminates every MicroVM and clears the pointer.

## The reviewer's first minute, the demo, and the package

**Cold path.** The page loads from CloudFront instantly and calls the session function. If a control plane is suspended, auto-resume wakes it in seconds and the page says the machine is waking. If none exists, the session function launches one from the snapshot and the page says the control plane is starting. Their tab's node joins, the control plane launches the two cores, and the page shows them arriving. Under thirty seconds from click to three nodes rendering. Warm path, someone else already there: instant.

**The demo, about five minutes.** One tab plus two cloud cores rendering. Two more real tabs join. Spawn ten, throughput climbs and the dashboard shows why it stops at the core count. Kill half, tiles flash and the frame completes. Freeze half, four seconds of silence, same result by the other detection path. Throttle half, twins appear and duplicates verify. Redundancy on, badges. Open the editor, change the palette in the Mandelbrot source, compile in the browser, launch, the cluster runs it. Switch to word count, three stages and a bar chart. Trigger a rotation, the banner, the reconnects, the render continues. Close with the ledger and files panels: hashes everywhere, no bytes in the control plane.

**Packaging.** README with what, why, architecture, in and out of scope, run and deploy. The rationale doc answering the five required questions. The video walking the script above. Transcripts exported into the docs folder. Secrets scan, license file, corpus attribution, and the repo goes public.

**Milestones, in fault-tolerant order,** each leaving something deployable: M0 skeleton and verification. M1 the machine: ledger, fill, liveness, verification, churn simulation, browser node, sandbox, Mandelbrot as a program, basic dashboard, local cores. M2 programs: planning as a task, the filesystem, word count, editor and in-browser compile, queue, views. M3 fleet: snapshots, handover, cloud cores, scale to zero, deploy as rotation. M4 polish and end-to-end tests. M5 package.

**One flag for the rationale, not for now.** The assignment asks for time spent and grades scoping against an eight-hour ceiling. This build is many days by design. The rationale has to own that choice plainly rather than round it down.

That closes the walkthrough. Everything settled is in the design record. What remains before M0 is on your side: create the private repo and log in with `gh`.

Good place to stop and settle it. Here is what exists, what I propose, and what I need from you.

## What is on this machine today

Your AWS config has several named profiles, with `default` pointing at us-west-2. I have looked only at profile names and regions. I have not read the credentials file and will not. There is no AWS CLI installed yet; it arrives through mise. So right now nothing I run can touch AWS, and the first command that does should be one we have agreed on.

## The two decisions

**1. Which account and which identity.**

| Option | What it means | Blast radius |
|---|---|---|
| A dedicated AWS account for this project | New account in your organization, budget attached, nothing else in it | Smallest. Going public later is safe by construction |
| A dedicated role in an existing account | An IAM role with a tight policy and a permission boundary, assumed from `default` through a `tabframe` profile | Small. Whatever `default` can do, the project identity cannot exceed the role |
| Use `default` as is | Whatever that key can do, I can do | Depends entirely on what `default` is. If it is admin or root, everything in the account is one typo away |

I recommend the first if you can create an account, otherwise the second. The profile would look like this, and mise sets `AWS_PROFILE=tabframe` so the raw key is never the working identity:

```ini
[profile tabframe]
role_arn        = arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/TabframeOperator
source_profile  = default
region          = us-west-2
duration_seconds = 3600
```

One constraint to know: if the role requires MFA to assume, the CDK cannot prompt for a code when I run it. Either the assume has no MFA condition, or you use IAM Identity Center and run `aws sso login` yourself before a session, or you export a session's credentials into the gitignored `.env.local` for an hour. Your call, and I'll fit the setup to it.

**2. How narrow the laptop identity is.** CDK's bootstrap model makes this easy: the identity that runs `cdk deploy` only needs to assume the CDK roles that bootstrap creates, and CloudFormation does the actual work under its own execution role. Everything else that mutates the account goes through the two fleet functions, which have their own roles. So the operator role needs exactly this:

- Assume the CDK deploy, file-publishing, and lookup roles.
- Invoke the two fleet functions.
- Read-only on Lambda MicroVMs, CloudFormation, CloudWatch Logs, Service Quotas, and the project buckets.

It cannot create, delete, or run anything directly. The image publish moves inside CloudFormation so it needs no extra rights. That is a real least-privilege story, and it costs nothing.

## Inside AWS

No static keys anywhere. Every component gets a role defined in CDK with only what it needs: the build role reads the artifact bucket, the execution role presigns uploads, writes snapshots, reads the pointer, and runs or terminates cores, the fleet roles run and terminate control planes, mint endpoint tokens, and write the pointer. The browser never holds AWS credentials. It gets JWE tokens scoped to one MicroVM and one port for at most an hour, and presigned S3 URLs scoped to one key with a pinned checksum and a short expiry.

- **Repo.** No keys, no account id, no email addresses. `.env.local` gitignored. CDK context that embeds the account id stays out of the repo, since it goes public later.

- **Control-plane execution role.** Puts to the blob bucket, which is what presigned uploads sign with. Reads and writes the snapshot bucket. Reads the SSM pointer. Runs, gets, lists, and terminates MicroVMs tagged as cores, and can pass the core role. Writes logs.
- **Core execution role.** Logs only. Cores need no AWS access at all; they talk to the control plane and the store like a browser does.
- **Session function role.** Mints endpoint tokens, reads one MicroVM, reads the pointer, may invoke rotate for healing.
- **Rotate function role.** Runs and terminates control planes, mints tokens for the handover calls, reads and writes the pointer, can pass the control-plane role.
- **CDK's own roles** from bootstrap. The CloudFormation execution role defaults to administrator, which is what lets a deploy create the roles above. That can be narrowed later, but it is the one place broad rights are conventional.

No IAM users for the application, no static keys anywhere, S3 buckets private behind CloudFront. One optional hardening if you want it: a scoped operator role assumed from the `tabframe` profile for day-to-day deploys, keeping the admin key for bootstrap only. ## Assistant · 2026-09-02T02:13:51.521Z

The region block is in and resolves correctly: the profile now defaults to us-west-2 with JSON output, so that item is closed.

**What the region block does.** Every AWS API call is made against one region, and Lambda MicroVMs, S3 buckets, and CloudFormation stacks all live in a specific one. Without a region on the profile, a CLI call fails with "you must specify a region," and CDK cannot infer its target environment from the profile. With it, any command using the `tabframe` profile lands in us-west-2 unless told otherwise. Mise sets `AWS_REGION` inside the repo as well, so there are now two layers saying the same thing, which is what you want when the wrong region means a stack in the wrong place. JSON output makes scripted parsing reliable.

**What the budget alarm is and why it needs two inputs from you.** AWS Budgets is a monthly spending ceiling on the account that sends a notification when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold. It is free for notification-only budgets. It is the backstop behind every cost guard in the design: idle suspend, cores scaling to zero, maximum durations. Those guards are code, and code has bugs. A rotation that fails to terminate the old control plane, or a fleet loop that keeps launching cores, would burn money quietly. The budget is the thing that tells a human.

- **The ceiling.** I'd set $25 a month. Expected spend is pennies while idle, about thirteen cents per active hour, and around three dollars for a full day of development with the machine awake. At $25 the alarm still catches a runaway within a day, with notifications at 50, 80, and 100 percent of actual spend plus the forecast crossing 100.
- **The address.** Notifications have to go somewhere, and that is an email address baked into infrastructure. Your global rule says I never put your address into code or config without asking, so I am asking. Options: your own address, a dedicated alerting address, or an SNS topic you subscribe to yourself. Wherever it comes from, it will not be committed. CDK reads it from the gitignored `.env.local` at synth time, so the public repo shows a variable name and no value, and the address exists only in the CloudFormation template inside your account.

One optional hardening worth considering here: a budget notification can also target an SNS topic, and a small Lambda subscribed to it can run the same logic as the kill switch, terminating every MicroVM and clearing the pointer when spend crosses 100 percent. That turns the alarm from "tell a human" into "stop the machine." Cheap to add, and it closes the last gap in the cost story.

So the two answers I need: the ceiling, if not $25, and the address, plus a yes or no on the automatic kill switch.

# Tabframe — Design Record

**Status:** design complete, build not started. Written 2026-09-01 during a full pre-build walkthrough.
This document is the source of truth for the build. It supersedes the earlier handoff and seed
documents wherever they differ.

**One line:** a fault-tolerant distributed computer whose cores are browser tabs and Firecracker
microVMs, programmed with WebAssembly modules, whose control plane holds only metadata and hashes,
and which stays correct while cores — and the control plane itself — come and go.

---

## Contents

1. Decisions register
2. The system in one page
3. Runtime picture
4. Nodes
5. Programs
6. The control plane
7. Data paths and the store
8. The wire
9. Hosting and fleet
10. Security and credentials
11. Tooling and repo
12. Tests and dev loop
13. Deploy, operations, and the reviewer's view
14. Milestones
15. Rationale hooks
16. Glossary
